newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY RULES HINDER DOMESTIC DERIV MKT-FOREX CLUB.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY RULES HINDER DOMESTIC DERIV MKT-FOREX CLUB.

text.p: Hungary's relatively less liberalised capital market may protect the economy from currency troubles but hinders the development of the domestic derivative market, the Hungarian Forex Club (MFT) said.
"London may become the main market of many forint-denominated derivative products," MFT President Sandor Sebok told a news conference.

The forint is convertible in all current account deals according to International Monetary Fund criteria and is also convertible for most long-term capital movements, but restrictions on short-term capital movements are still in place.

In the past year, the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) has increased the stability of the financial market by cautious policies, following the movements of market interest rates and inflation by cutting its own rates in small steps, Sebok said.

While the NBH will loosen certain capital movement rules in 1998, it does not plan to allow the inflow of foreign investments in short-term instruments such as derivatives and short maturity securities, in order to protect the forint, he said.

Recent currency turbulences in the more liberalised Czech and Polish markets, partly due to a flight of short-term foreign capital, may justify the NBH's cautious stance from a macroeconomic point of view, he said.

However, this conservative attitude may have a negative impact oh Hungarian financial institutions, which are not able to benefit from a heavily increased foreign interest in Hungarian derivative products which serve to hedge exchange rate risks, Sebok said.
MFT official Geza Egyed added that the interest of foreign investors in forint derivatives has also strengthened substantially.
"Margins in large western currencies are already so narrow that the investors are looking at other currencies," he said.
Egyed said that a market of forint-denominated non-deliverable forward deals (NFDs) appeared in London a few months ago and the daily turnover there has already reached $50 million.
"I think the interest in NFD's will increase," he said. "Many banks are just now setting up their NFD desks just now."
He added that turnover on the London market was unlikely to become large enough to influence the Hungarian economy as a whole, but it represented lost business to the Hungarian financial sector.
